topic.examWeightHint: A Higher-only outcome and, in two of the last three series, the hardest question on the B1 Higher paper. mustMemorise: Nitrogen fixation: nitrogen gas → nitrates, by nitrogen-fixing bacteria (soil, root nodules of legumes, and lightning)
Decomposition: protein in dead material and urea → ammonium compounds, by decomposing bacteria and fungi
Nitrification: ammonium → nitrites → nitrates, by nitrifying bacteria, AEROBIC
Denitrification: nitrates → nitrogen gas, by denitrifying bacteria, ANAEROBIC
The process ends in -ation or -ition; the bacteria end in -ing
Plants absorb NITRATES through their roots to make amino acids and proteins
Waterlogged: no air spaces → no oxygen → denitrifying bacteria multiply → nitrate lost as nitrogen gas

Chemical or ionic equations for any of the four processes

Ammonification as a separate named process

noteBlocks.lede: Living things need nitrogen to build protein, but the nitrogen in the air is useless to them until bacteria change it. Four processes move nitrogen round the soil, each carried out by its own type of bacteria, and how wet the soil is decides which of them wins.

noteBlocks.md: Four-fifths of the air is nitrogen and plants cannot use any of it. Bacteria in the soil do the conversion for them, turning nitrogen gas into nitrate, while other bacteria turn it back again.

noteBlocks.alt: The nitrogen cycle drawn as seven boxes joined by eight arrows. Nitrogen gas in the air becomes nitrates in the soil by nitrogen fixation carried out by nitrogen-fixing bacteria and by lightning. Nitrates are absorbed by roots and used to make protein in plants. Feeding passes that protein to animals. Death, excretion and egestion send protein to dead matter and waste. Decomposition by decomposing bacteria and fungi turns it into ammonium compounds. Nitrification by nitrifying bacteria turns ammonium into nitrites and then nitrates. Denitrification by denitrifying bacteria turns nitrates back into nitrogen gas in waterlogged, anaerobic conditions. A footnote marks nitrite and lightning as background beyond this specification.

noteBlocks.title: The one rule that carries this topic
noteBlocks.md:
**Learn every arrow as a pair: the process, and the bacteria.**

• **nitrogen fixation** — *nitrogen-fixing* bacteria
• **decomposition** — *decomposing* (saprophytic) bacteria and fungi
• **nitrification** — *nitrifying* bacteria
• **denitrification** — *denitrifying* bacteria

The names of individual species are **not** required. What is required is the ability to give the process in one part and the type of bacteria in the next, without swapping them over.

noteBlocks.prompt: Bacteria that change nitrogen gas from the air into nitrates are called ______ bacteria.
noteBlocks.explain: Nitrogen-fixing. Fixing means taking something out of the air and locking it into a compound — the same word is used for carbon fixation in photosynthesis.

noteBlocks.text: The four processes, one at a time

noteBlocks.md: **1 Nitrogen fixation.** The air is about four-fifths **nitrogen gas**, but plants cannot use it: the molecule is too unreactive. **nitrogen-fixing bacteria** turn it into **nitrates**, which plants can absorb. Some live free in the soil; others live inside **root nodules** on the roots of **legumes** — clover, peas, beans — where they get sugars from the plant and give it nitrate in return. **Lightning** fixes a little nitrogen too.

noteBlocks.alt: Close-up photograph of a legume root system lifted from the soil. Pale branching roots carry a scattering of rounded, pinkish-brown swellings a few millimetres across, spaced along the thicker roots, with fine root hairs and soil grains around them
noteBlocks.caption: Root nodules on a legume, lifted straight out of the soil. Each pinkish swelling is a chamber full of nitrogen-fixing bacteria that the plant houses and feeds.
noteBlocks.prompt: Name the type of bacteria living inside these swellings, name the process they carry out, and state what the plant gains from housing them.

noteBlocks.title: Why a plant cannot use the nitrogen it is standing in
noteBlocks.md: Nitrogen gas is two atoms locked together so tightly that nothing in a plant can pull them apart. Plants need nitrogen as **nitrate** instead, a soluble ion the roots can absorb and build into amino acids.

noteBlocks.prompt: Where on a clover plant do the nitrogen-fixing bacteria live?
noteBlocks.explain: In root nodules on the roots of legumes — clover, peas and beans.

noteBlocks.md: **2 Decomposition.** When plants and animals die, and whenever animals produce **urine and faeces**, the **protein** and **urea** in that material is broken down by **decomposing (saprophytic) bacteria and fungi** into **ammonium compounds** in the soil. This is the step that Summer 2025's candidates most often left unnamed.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which process turns the protein in dead material into ammonium compounds?
noteBlocks.explain: Decomposition, by saprophytic bacteria and fungi.

noteBlocks.md: **3 Nitrification.** **nitrifying bacteria** oxidise those **ammonium compounds** into **nitrites** and then into **nitrates**. They are **aerobic**, so they need soil with **air spaces** — which is why a waterlogged field makes less nitrate as well as losing what it has.

**4 Denitrification.** **denitrifying bacteria** do the opposite: they turn **nitrates back into nitrogen gas**, which is lost to the air. They are **anaerobic**, so they multiply exactly where the others are struggling — in **waterlogged soil**.

Only denitrification is marked as not needing air. A footnote marks nitrite as background beyond this specification.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which process turns ammonium compounds into nitrates?
noteBlocks.explain: Nitrification, by nitrifying bacteria. Denitrification runs the other way and produces nitrogen gas; decomposition is the step before, which makes the ammonium in the first place.

noteBlocks.md:
Write the waterlogging answer as a **chain**, one link per mark:

**1** The soil is waterlogged, so the **air spaces are full of water**.
**2** There is therefore **little or no oxygen** — conditions are **anaerobic**.
**3** **Nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria are aerobic**, so they become less active and **less nitrate is made**.
**4** **Denitrifying bacteria are anaerobic**, so they multiply and **turn more nitrate into nitrogen gas**.
**5** So there is **less nitrate available to plants**, and less protein can be made.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why is a waterlogged soil short of oxygen?
options: the plants use it all up
it is too cold for air to dissolve
noteBlocks.explain: Water fills the spaces between the soil grains, so conditions become anaerobic.

noteBlocks.title: March 2026 B1 Higher Q7 — the hardest question on the paper
noteBlocks.md: Parts (d) and (e) asked candidates to **name the types of nitrogen bacteria** and **explain why waterlogged soil leaves plants short of nitrate**. The Chief Examiner reported both as the most challenging on the paper, and added that in part (d) **candidates lost marks by naming the processes when the question asked for the types of bacteria**. Read the command word twice: *nitrification* and *nitrifying bacteria* are not interchangeable.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why does a waterlogged field lose nitrate?
options: the air spaces fill with water, so anaerobic denitrifying bacteria thrive and turn nitrate into nitrogen gas
the nitrate is washed downwards out of reach of the roots only
the nitrifying bacteria turn the nitrate back into ammonium
noteBlocks.answer: the air spaces fill with water, so anaerobic denitrifying bacteria thrive and turn nitrate into nitrogen gas
noteBlocks.explain: Leaching does happen, but the answer the scheme wants is the bacteria: no oxygen means denitrifying bacteria multiply, and nitrate leaves as nitrogen gas. Nitrifying bacteria never run backwards.

noteBlocks.md: Plants absorb **nitrates** through their roots and use them to make **amino acids** and then **proteins** — for growth, for enzymes, for everything. More nitrate therefore means more growth, until the plants cannot take in any more. Here the yield climbs by **50%** from no fertiliser to low, and by **25%** from low to medium, but only by **0.2 tonnes per hectare** from medium to high. The reason for the flat top is exactly the sentence March 2026's report says only the more able candidates wrote: **the plants cannot absorb any more nitrate**.

noteBlocks.prompt: The yield rose from 4.8 to 6 tonnes per hectare. Calculate the percentage increase.
noteBlocks.explain: (6 − 4.8) ÷ 4.8 × 100 = 1.2 ÷ 4.8 × 100 = 25%. Dividing by 6 instead would give 20%, which is the error the March 2026 report names.

noteBlocks.title: Not on this specification
noteBlocks.md: You do **not** need the names of individual bacteria (*Rhizobium*, *Nitrosomonas*, *Nitrobacter*), the chemical equations of any of these reactions, the Haber process, or eutrophication as part of *this* outcome — eutrophication is outcome 1.7.12 and has its own topic. What you do need is the four processes, the four types of bacteria, and the aerobic or anaerobic condition each one needs.

the nodules contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria

parts.stem: One nitrogen atom travels round the cycle. Put these five stages in order, starting in the air.

items: The atom is part of a nitrogen molecule in the air
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria turn it into nitrate in the soil
A grass plant absorbs the nitrate and builds it into protein
The grass dies and decomposing bacteria turn its protein into ammonium compounds
Nitrifying bacteria turn the ammonium back into nitrate

scheme.for: nitrogen fixation comes first, out of the air
absorption and protein-building by the plant comes next
decomposition to ammonium follows the plant's death
nitrification turns the ammonium back into nitrate

hints: Nitrogen can only leave the air by one route.
Ammonium always comes before nitrate, never after.
parts.workedSolution: The atom starts as part of a nitrogen molecule in the air. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert it into nitrate in the soil. A grass plant absorbs the nitrate and builds it into protein. The grass dies and decomposing bacteria turn that protein into ammonium compounds. Nitrifying bacteria then turn the ammonium back into nitrate.

pattern.regex: nitrifying bacteria turn the ammonium[^;\n]{0,60}dies and decomposing

commonErrors.feedback: Ammonium has to be made by decomposition before nitrifying bacteria can work on it. Decomposition always comes first.

context.setting: A soil scientist measuring oxygen at three depths

figures.alt: Two soil columns: a well-drained soil with the spaces between its grains drawn open, and a waterlogged soil with those spaces tinted to show water filling them.

parts.stem: State which of the four nitrogen-cycle processes needs anaerobic conditions.

accepted: denitrification

scheme.for: denitrification

hints: Only one of the four works without oxygen.
parts.workedSolution: Denitrification.

commonErrors.feedback: Nitrification is aerobic and needs air spaces. Denitrification is the anaerobic one.

parts.stem: Oxygen in a soil falls steadily with depth. Explain what this means for the nitrate content deep in that soil.

accepted: deeper down there is less oxygen, so nitrifying bacteria are less active and make less nitrate while denitrifying bacteria become more active and remove nitrate, so the nitrate content is lower deeper down

scheme.for: deeper soil has less oxygen, so conditions become anaerobic
denitrifying bacteria are anaerobic, so they become more active and convert nitrate into nitrogen gas
nitrifying bacteria are aerobic, so less nitrate is made, and the nitrate content is lower with depth

hints: Which bacteria gain as the oxygen falls, and which lose?
parts.workedSolution: As oxygen falls with depth the soil becomes anaerobic. Denitrifying bacteria are anaerobic, so they become more active deeper down and convert nitrate into nitrogen gas. Nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria are aerobic, so they become less active and make less nitrate. The nitrate content is therefore lower the deeper you go.

pattern.regex: more nitrate deeper|nitrate increases with depth

commonErrors.feedback: Less oxygen means more denitrification and less nitrification, so the nitrate falls rather than rises with depth.

parts.stem: Suggest why ploughing a field helps to keep its nitrate content up.

accepted: ploughing breaks the soil up and lets air into it, so the aerobic nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria stay active and the anaerobic denitrifying bacteria do not take over

scheme.for: ploughing breaks the soil up and lets air, and so oxygen, into it
the aerobic nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria stay active while the anaerobic denitrifying bacteria do not

hints: What does turning the soil over do to the spaces between the grains?
parts.workedSolution: Ploughing breaks up the soil and opens air spaces, so oxygen reaches the bacteria. The aerobic nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria stay active and keep making nitrate, while the anaerobic denitrifying bacteria are held back and less nitrate is lost as nitrogen gas.

context.setting: A sheep grazing a hillside, and the nitrogen in the grass it eats

parts.stem:
A sheep grazes a hillside. Nitrogen from the air ends up in the sheep's muscle protein, and later returns to the air.
Describe and explain the journey of that nitrogen, naming the processes and the types of bacteria involved.

Your written communication is assessed in this question, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: nitrogen gas in the air is converted into nitrates by nitrogen fixation
this is done by nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the soil and in the root nodules of legumes
grass absorbs the nitrates through its roots and uses them to make protein
the sheep eats the grass and digests the plant protein into amino acids, which it builds into its own protein
the sheep's urine, faeces and eventually its body return protein and urea to the soil
decomposing bacteria and fungi break that down into ammonium compounds
nitrifying bacteria convert the ammonium into nitrates (by way of nitrites, which this specification does not require), and they are aerobic
denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas, and they are anaerobic

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Every arrow is a pair: name the process and name the bacteria.
Finish in the air, because the question says the nitrogen returns there.
parts.workedSolution: Nitrogen gas makes up most of the air, but grass cannot use it. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, some free in the soil and some in the root nodules of legumes growing on the hillside, carry out nitrogen fixation and convert the gas into nitrates. The grass absorbs those nitrates through its roots and uses them to make amino acids and then protein. The sheep eats the grass, digests the plant protein into amino acids and builds its own muscle protein from them. The sheep's urine and faeces, and eventually its body, return protein and urea to the soil, where decomposing bacteria and fungi break them down into ammonium compounds. Nitrifying bacteria, which are aerobic, then convert the ammonium into nitrates — by way of nitrites, a step this specification does not require. Finally denitrifying bacteria, which are anaerobic and thrive in waterlogged ground, convert some of those nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air.

commonErrors.feedback: Every process has been named but no bacteria. Half the indicative points here are the types of bacteria, so naming them doubles the available credit.
The ammonium step is missing: decomposition produces ammonium compounds, and nitrification turns those into nitrate. Going straight from dead matter to nitrate loses two points.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ruairí is asked: 'Name the types of bacteria at arrows P, Q and R on the nitrogen cycle. P: nitrogen gas → nitrate. Q: ammonium → nitrate. R: nitrate → nitrogen gas. [3]'
His answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 gives a **process**, and the question asked for the **type of bacteria**. P should be **nitrogen-fixing bacteria**; lines 2 and 3 name the bacteria correctly. March 2026's Chief Examiner named this exact slip: *candidates lost marks by naming the processes when the question asked for the types of bacteria*.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks from three, and the biology behind every answer was right. The fix is a reading habit, not a revision one: underline the noun in the question — *process* or *bacteria* — before you write. The pattern is regular, so it costs nothing to learn: the process ends in **-ation** or **-ition**, the bacteria end in **-ing**.

findTheMistake.stem:
Méabh is asked: 'Explain why a waterlogged soil contains less nitrate. [3]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: The soil is full of water so all the nitrate is washed away.
The nitrifying bacteria then turn the nitrate back into nitrogen gas.
So there is less nitrate for the plants.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: **Nitrifying** bacteria *make* nitrate; it is **denitrifying** bacteria that turn it back into nitrogen gas. Line 1 is also weak: washing away does happen, but the marking points are about **oxygen** — water fills the air spaces, so the soil becomes **anaerobic**, and the **anaerobic denitrifying bacteria** multiply while the **aerobic nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria** slow down.
correction: The water fills the air spaces in the soil, so there is little or no oxygen and the soil becomes anaerobic.
Denitrifying bacteria are anaerobic, so they multiply and turn nitrates into nitrogen gas.
The aerobic nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria become less active, so less new nitrate is made and there is less for the plants.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark from three, for the first line — 'full of water' is the start of the oxygen point, though it stops short of saying the oxygen has gone. The single word that costs the other two is the missing **de-**. A check that works under pressure: nitrate has to come from somewhere, so a process whose name contains **nitr** and **-ation** with no **de-** must be *making* it. Then build the answer as a chain — no air spaces, no oxygen, denitrifying bacteria multiply, nitrate leaves as gas — and each link is a mark.

prompts.prompt: Name the four processes of the nitrogen cycle.
Name the four types of bacteria, one for each process.
prompts.answer: Nitrogen-fixing, decomposing (saprophytic), nitrifying and denitrifying bacteria.

prompts.prompt: What does nitrogen fixation change, and into what?
prompts.answer: Nitrogen gas from the air into nitrates, which plants can absorb. It is done by nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the soil and in root nodules, and by lightning. (Lightning is background only: this specification asks for the bacteria.)

prompts.prompt: What does decomposition change, and into what?
prompts.answer: Protein in dead material and urea in waste into ammonium compounds, by decomposing (saprophytic) bacteria and fungi.

prompts.prompt: What does nitrification change, and into what?
prompts.answer: Ammonium compounds into nitrites and then into nitrates, by nitrifying bacteria. They are aerobic. (Not on this specification: the nitrite step — CCEA asks only for ammonium compounds → nitrates.)

prompts.prompt: What does denitrification change, and into what?
prompts.answer: Nitrates back into nitrogen gas, by denitrifying bacteria. They are anaerobic.

prompts.prompt: Explain, as a chain, why a waterlogged soil loses nitrate.
prompts.answer: The air spaces fill with water, so there is no oxygen; denitrifying bacteria are anaerobic so they multiply and convert nitrate into nitrogen gas; the aerobic nitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria become less active, so less nitrate is made; so there is less nitrate for plants.

prompts.prompt: What do plants use nitrate for, and how do animals get their nitrogen?
prompts.answer: Plants absorb nitrate through their roots and use it to make amino acids and then proteins. Animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals and digesting their protein.

prompts.prompt: A question asks for the TYPE OF BACTERIA. What must your answer end in?
prompts.answer: -ing: nitrogen-fixing, nitrifying, denitrifying, decomposing. Processes end in -ation or -ition, and giving a process where bacteria were asked for earns nothing.

prompts.prompt: Why does a farmer sow clover in a field for a season?
prompts.answer: Clover is a legume with root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria, which convert nitrogen gas into nitrate and raise the soil's nitrate content for the next crop.
